newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia share rally falters but profit-taking light.
newsitem.headline: Russia share rally falters but profit-taking light.

text.p: The recent rally in Russian shares took a pause for breath on light profit-taking on Wednesday but many analysts said the market was not on the edge of an end-of-year sell-off.
"The market has had a solid 10 percent rally in the last two weeks and there were a few profit-takers around, mainly Russians," said Martin Diggle of Brunswick.
Despite dealer sentiment that the market had lost ground, the Russian Trading System index inched up 0.28 percent to 190.74 on $19 million volume, healthy though lower than over the last week.
Recent favorites such as Rostelekom ordinaries and preferred and Surgutneftegaz were leading losers for the day.
Rostelekom ordinaries edged down to $2.61 from $2.67, prefs to $2.040 from $2.202 and Surgut ordinaries to $0.43 from $0.44.
"People are trying to figure out the appropriate level of discount on the preferreds," Diggle said, explaining losses by a number of prefs which have gained steadily recently.
CentreInvest research chief James Fenkner said high volumes indicated the market was not ready to stall. "Volumes tend to lead prices," he said.
"The last seven days had average volumes of $24 million. We see the index much higher next week."
He did not see major end of the year sell-offs in store.
But analysts said some investors were repositioning towards less well known local utilities, phone companies and oil companies.
Alfa-Capital trader Alexander Bubnovsky said larger investors were holding firm while some traders and smaller investors moved out.
"Smaller investors who shouldn't be in Russia in the first place will be selling," he said.
Fenkner said leading stocks would not languish because they had achieved a critical mass of analyst-followers.
"Every Russian analyst knows something about Mosenergo. How many know about the energos around the golden ring of Moscow -- like Vladimir or Tver?" he said.
More sophisticated investors are certainly heading for the hinterland, though. "Whether Yeltsin is coming or going, we are looking at company fundamentals," said one London equity analyst.
